perArtifact.deficiency: The assessment structure is mechanically repetitive and under-specified: it lists 45 near-identical weekly items instead of a meaningful progression or distinct grading criteria.
The instructional arc is generic and thin on actual Mandarin practice, with repeated placeholder-style activities that do not clearly move students from numbers to age and dates.
It is mostly a template filled with broad statements and repetitive prompts, with too little concrete direction-language practice to function as a real class plan.
The content is usable, but it is not yet clean student-facing material because it mixes explanatory prose with awkward 'students think' phrasing and has some duplication.
The grading schema is oddly redundant and mechanically generated, with duplicated weekly quiz/lab rows and no real explanation of how the components fit pedagogically.
The plan is strong, but it is overly scripted and repeats a few ideas in a way that feels templated rather than naturally sequenced for teaching.
It has a clear arc, but the recursive examples are somewhat narrow and the session leans too heavily on trace-following instead of building broader conceptual flexibility.
The items are well aligned, but the applied question is a little under-specified because it asks for a corrected program without presenting a fully rigorous target form.
It is useful but thin: mostly definitions and recall prompts, with too little varied practice to support independent study at the level of the lesson.
The assessment plan is not operationalized: every weekly lab row uses the same placeholder label, so a professor cannot tell what is being graded or how the 14 lab assessments actually differ.
The lesson is too generic and templated; the activities never specify concrete specimens, lab procedures, or eruption-case evidence students would actually work with.
It is heavily scripted and repetitive, so the core definition is restated more than the lab work is developed into a sharper observation-to-application sequence.
It is too thin for a weekly geology study guide: one key-concept row and two near-duplicate recall questions do not give enough retrieval practice or differentiation.
The reading architecture is incomplete: many sessions list placeholders or no readings at all, and the required-texts section names only one work despite the course overview naming many texts.

The materials/source setup is not clean: the lesson is built around Du Fu and Li Bai, but the materials table is malformed and the primary text packet is too thin to support the session without edits.
The lesson cites the wrong required text basis: it lists Laura Riding in Materials but teaches The Waste Land throughout, so the session is not source-aligned as written.
The quiz is mostly recall and restatement of the lesson’s own examples, with limited independent transfer or discriminating application beyond the scripted corrections.
It duplicates the lesson too closely instead of condensing into a study aid, and it also inherits the same text mismatch between the listed reading and the Eliot-centered content.
The course description, grading scheme, and schedule do not fully align, and the repeated weekly image-analysis rows read like templated filler rather than a coherent assessment structure.
It is strong and teachable, but it is overly scripted and generic in places, relying on labeled image routines without naming specific artworks or sources for the analysis.
The session arc is essentially placeholder text, with vague activities that do not concretely specify what students will do, see, or produce.
It overcompresses Romanticism and Realism into a few memorization points and gives Realism too little visual and historical specificity.
It is a usable course skeleton, but too many sessions have no readings and the repeated weekly-argument-analysis assessments are not differentiated enough to show a concrete instructional arc.

The main weakness is sourcing and textual grounding: it leans on a well-built activity sequence, but the primary text is not fully integrated with a clear citation/locator and the Descartes excerpt is only loosely framed.

It flattens distinct philosophical moves into one streamlined framework, so Rawls, social contract, and distributive justice are treated a bit too generically rather than with enough conceptual nuance.
It mostly repeats the lesson plan instead of adding fresh explanation, examples, or contrastive guidance that would deepen student understanding.
